planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural winter stratification, or set container-grown plants in spring in lean, sharply drained, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun.

directions: Drummond's mountain avens is a mat-forming, woody-based perennial native to glacial outwash, gravel bars, and cobble beaches across the boreal north, including stretches of the Lake Superior shoreline, where its nitrogen-fixing roots let it colonize raw, mineral soil ahead of most other plants. Nodding, bell-shaped yellow flowers that never fully open stand just above trailing, oak-shaped leaves in early summer, followed by long, silvery, plumose seed heads that catch light like small feather dusters. The wiry, creeping stems root as they spread, slowly building a tough, drought-tolerant mat over lean ground. Give it full sun and sharp drainage in a rock garden, gravel bed, or slope, since it resents heavy, wet soils.

planting.note: Root hardwood or softwood cuttings directly in moist soil, or set container-grown plants in spring in constantly moist to wet, calcareous soil in full sun to light shade.

directions: Hoary willow is a northern wetland shrub whose young stems and narrow leaves are coated in dense white, woolly hairs that give the whole plant a silvery-gray cast, especially striking in the calcareous fens, swamp edges, and marly shorelines around the upper Great Lakes. Small gray-and-yellow catkins open before the leaves in earliest spring, an important early nectar source. Left alone it forms an upright, suckering thicket useful for stabilizing wet shorelines and pond margins. Give it constantly moist to wet, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun to light shade, where it tolerates occasional flooding better than most garden shrubs.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall or very early spring directly onto well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun, since the fleshy roots resent transplanting once established.

directions: Oysterleaf is a trailing coastal perennial native to cobble and gravel beaches of the far north, with isolated populations on the Lake Superior shoreline well south of its main Arctic and subarctic range. Thick, fleshy, blue-green leaves have a glaucous, rippled surface reminiscent of an oyster shell, and loose clusters of small, pink-budded flowers open sky blue, like a sprawling miniature Virginia bluebells. The trailing stems hug bare sand and gravel, tolerating salt spray, storm wash, and lean soil that would kill most perennials outright. Sow seed directly where it is to grow, in well-drained sandy or gravelly soil in full sun, and avoid rich garden soil, which encourages rot rather than vigor.
